title: President of the European Central Bank Christine Lagarde to stand down in February
description: Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank (ECB), during a rates decision news conference in Frankfurt, Germany, on Thursday, June 11,
body: Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank (ECB), during a rates decision news conference in Frankfurt, Germany, on Thursday, June 11, 2026. Alex Kraus | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesEuropean Central Bank said on Thursday that President Christine Lagarde will step down from her role on Feb. 7 next year. Lagarde was given a standing ovation by the Governing Council of the euro area's central bank, which she has led since July 2019. Her term was due to end in October 2027. The announcement came ahead of the ECB's latest interest rate decision, due later on Thursday. European Council President Antonio Costa thanked Lagarde for her "dedication.""Through a global pandemic, a war in Europe, energy crises and inflation shocks, she has provided a steady and determined stewardship, helping to safeguard stability and the resilience of the euro area," Costa said in a statement.  The process of appointing her successor will begin immediately, he added.Lagarde, born in Paris in 1956, first worked as a high-ranking lawyer before joining the French government. In 2007, she became the first female Finance Minister of a G7 country. She was appointed managing director of the International Monetary Fund in 2011 before joining the ECB.Lagarde is viewed as a top candidate to become the next chair of the World Economic Forum, according to Financial Times reporting. In recent media interviews, she has suggested she does not plan a run at the French presidency in the 2027 election. This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.

schema.headline: President of the European Central Bank Christine Lagarde to stand down in February

title: Restaurant Brands reports mixed results as Burger King's U.S. turnaround shows signs of success
description: In this photo illustration, a Burger King Whopper and fries are seen in a restaurant on August 17, 2026, in Hollywood, Florida. Joe Raedle | Getty Ima
body: In this photo illustration, a Burger King Whopper and fries are seen in a restaurant on August 17, 2026, in Hollywood, Florida. Joe Raedle | Getty ImagesRestaurant Brands International on Thursday reported mixed quarterly results as Popeyes' struggles offset Burger King's successful U.S. turnaround. Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $1.10 adjusted vs. $1.09 expectedRevenue: $2.53 billion vs. $2.54 billion expectedRestaurant Brands reported fiscal third-quarter net income attributable to common shareholders of $542 million, or $1.54 per share, up from $315 million, or 96 cents per share, a year earlier.Excluding certain non-cash items, the company earned $1.10 per share.Net revenue rose 3.1% to $2.53 billion. Across all of its restaurants, the company reported same-store sales growth of 3.8%.Burger King was the top performer, with U.S. same-store sales growth of 8.4%. The burger chain's home market is in the middle of multiyear turnaround, with a focus on improving its food and restaurants. Tim Hortons reported same-store sales growth of 1.8% in Canada, its home market. Popeyes was once again the laggard of Restaurant Brands' portfolio. The fried chicken chain's U.S. same-store sales fell 2.2%. In recent quarters, Popeyes has struggled as other chicken rivals have lured its customers away with discounts. Restaurant Brands is trying to stage a comeback with improved restaurant operations and a focus on its core menu.The company's international business saw same-store sales growth of 3.9%, fueled by its Burger King locations.

schema.headline: Restaurant Brands reports mixed results as Burger King's U.S. turnaround shows signs of success

title: Nvidia's $12.9 billion Hugging Face deal draws DOJ scrutiny
description: Jensen Huang, co-founder, president and CEO of Nvidia, gestures during a press briefing in Paris on Oct. 13, 2026.Joel Saget | AFP | Getty ImagesNvidi
body: Jensen Huang, co-founder, president and CEO of Nvidia, gestures during a press briefing in Paris on Oct. 13, 2026.Joel Saget | AFP | Getty ImagesNvidia is facing questions from the U.S. Department of Justice concerning its acquisition of Hugging Face, an open-source platform for hosting and testing AI models, and how that deal may impact competitors in the field.CNBC has confirmed the probe with a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Reuters first reported the DOJ's inquiry on Wednesday. Nvidia announced its nearly $13 billion acquisition of Hugging Face in September, and at the time, CEO Jensen Huang wrote that the deal would help "expand access to AI for developers and institutions worldwide."Hugging Face already had massive adoption. At the time of the deal, Nvidia said in a press statement that more than 18 million people and more than 200,000 companies reportedly used Hugging Face to share at least 3 million models and 500,000 datasets.Hugging Face also sells infrastructure and collaboration tools to organizations working with closed, proprietary AI including chip companies. The Hugging Face acquisition marked Nvidia's second-biggest purchase, after it paid $20 billion for Groq assets at the end of last year, a deal that has also attracted DOJ scrutiny. The closest comparable to Hugging Face's business was GitHub, a software repository that was acquired by Microsoft in 2018 for $7.5 billion. Hugging Face gained renewed recognition after reports that OpenAI agents attacked the platform during testing.The company and that incident are part of a new, Netflix "insta-documentary" called "AI Gone Rogue."Nvidia declined to comment.

schema.headline: Nvidia's $12.9 billion Hugging Face deal draws DOJ scrutiny

title: Eli Lilly is about to report earnings. Here's what to expect
description: The Eli Lilly logo appears on the company’s office in San Diego, California, Nov. 21, 2025.Mike Blake | ReutersEli Lilly is slated to report third-qua
body: The Eli Lilly logo appears on the company’s office in San Diego, California, Nov. 21, 2025.Mike Blake | ReutersEli Lilly is slated to report third-quarter earnings and revenue on Thursday, which will likely be fueled by its blockbuster obesity drug Zepbound and diabetes counterpart Mounjaro. Here's what Wall Street is expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $6.26 expectedRevenue: $22.61 billion expectedBut investors will also be laser-focused on the launch of the company's obesity pill, Foundayo, which entered the market in April. Analysts forecast around $229 million in sales for the pill, StreetAccount estimates showed. Lilly's massive diabetes and obesity windfall – and dominance over chief rival Novo – show no signs of slowing down, even as the company grapples with lower net prices in the U.S. The pharma giant is converting these historic profits into a major dealmaking spree, striking a deal to buy a psychedelics drugmaker in July and announcing plans to purchase three vaccine makers in May.

schema.headline: Eli Lilly is about to report earnings. Here's what to expect

title: Alphabet falls 10% in premarket, putting it on course for its biggest ever post-earnings drop
description: The Google headquarters in Mountain View, California, US, on Tuesday, July 21, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAlphabet shares were s
body: The Google headquarters in Mountain View, California, US, on Tuesday, July 21, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAlphabet shares were sharply down in premarket trading on Thursday while Microsoft rose as investors focused on the tech giants' latest spending and free cash flow numbers in their third-quarter earnings.Alphabet was 10% lower in premarket trade while Microsoft was nearly 4% higher.If Alphabet closes more than 9.77% lower on Thursday, it would be its worst post-earnings reaction ever. The company went public in 2004.Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases during the third quarter, which was 30% higher than a year ago, but below analyst projections of $50.67 billion. Free cash flow fell 27% to $18.63 billion but remained positive.Alphabet, in contrast, reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion for the third quarter, which fell much further than the $2.70 billion analysts expected by analysts. The Google parent maintained its full year capital expenditure guidance of between $195 billion and $205 billion.The earnings report comes as investors scrutinize AI spending plans of tech companies and are focusing on the returns on those investments. "Microsoft is building out its architecture in a measured way and as such contains fewer surprises," Ben Barringer, global head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said on Thursday. "Alphabet, by contrast, saw its share price hit after hours as a result of a fairly messy set of results and a poorly handled earnings call," Barringer added.Nasdaq-100 futures were down more than 1% early Thursday.Search under pressureAlphabet's biggest source of revenue, search advertising, grew 12% in the September quarter to $63.35 billion, but missed analyst expectations, adding further pressure to the company's shares.Philipp Schindler, Alphabet's chief business officer, said the impact on the search business was partly because of lower monetization within the company's AI Mode. He added that Alphabet is now "scaling" ads within its AI Overviews and AI Mode products, including in international markets. Google's search business has faced headwinds from the rise of other AI chatbots like OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. People may be carrying out more search queries outside Google. Gemini, Google's own AI chatbot, has failed to keep pace."The problem for Google is it faces an innovator's dilemma and doesn't know whether to protect its core business or look to join the disruption. As such, Google has lost its edge with Gemini and is behind peers on agentic AI," Barringer said.- CNBC's Robert Hum, Samantha Subin and Jordan Novet contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Alphabet falls 10% in premarket, putting it on course for its biggest ever post-earnings drop

title: Putin praises Elon Musk as a ‘real genius’ as Russia develops Starlink alternative
description: Russian President Vladimir Putin has called SpaceX CEO Elon Musk a "genius," as he revealed the two are in "close contact" about developing a Russian
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has called SpaceX CEO Elon Musk a "genius," as he revealed the two are in "close contact" about developing a Russian alternative to Starlink."Elon Musk is a genius, truly a genius," Putin said at the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on Wednesday. "He has already had more than 5,000 such satellites in orbit, while we are only taking the first steps," he said at an event where he discussed Russia's own satellite connectivity project, Rassvet.Rassvet is a satellite internet constellation in low Earth orbit, built by the Russian private aerospace company Bureau 1440."We are proud that we have begun doing this and that we have started doing it independently," Putin said according to a translation. "We are in close contact with our U.S. partners, including Mr Musk."  "In orbit, it is very important not to interfere with one another and to adhere to certain rules, discipline, and order. Both we and our U.S. partners value this mutual understanding. Together with Mr. Musk, despite all the political issues, we continue to work closely."SpaceX, Starlink's owner, didn't immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment. Starlink operates a constellation of more than 11,000 satellites in orbit, providing high-speed internet access to 174 countries, according to the company. The service drew attention earlier this month after Ukraine accused SpaceX and Musk of imposing restrictions that slowed the country's military satellite internet access, thereby harming its defensive capabilities. The restrictions affected Starshield, SpaceX’s satellite communications service for governments, causing drones and other moving terminals to lose or experience degraded connectivity above roughly 100 miles per hour, according to Ukrainian officials.President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed the restricted service for disrupting its air defense capabilities during frequent Russian air attacks.Musk has said Starshield is controlled by the U.S. government, and ultimately the president, while other reports have said the restriction was imposed by Musk. U.S. President Donald Trump has denied ordering the restriction.The White House and SpaceX did not respond to CNBC requests for comment on whether the service had been limited and where such an order came from.Musk later said Ukraine had breached Starlink's terms of service by using a civilian commercial network for offensive drone strikes. Ukraine has denied doing so.

schema.headline: Putin praises Elon Musk as a ‘real genius’ as Russia develops Starlink alternative

title: Weil, Gotshal & Manges, longtime Wall Street law firm, plans wind down
description: The logo of law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges LLP is seen outside of their office in Washington, D.C., U.S., Aug. 31, 2020.Andrew Kelly | ReutersA manag
body: The logo of law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges LLP is seen outside of their office in Washington, D.C., U.S., Aug. 31, 2020.Andrew Kelly | ReutersA management committee of Weil, Gotshal & Manges, the long-time Wall Street law firm, has recommended that its partners wind down operations, the firm said Wednesday.The recommendation came after an exodus of partners and the reported end, days ago, of talks with Willkie Farr & Gallagher about a potential merger. Weil, which has about 1,200 lawyers, in 2025 reportedly had more than $2 billion in revenue across multi-national operations."For more than 90 years, Weil, Gotshal & Manges has had the privilege of advising clients on some of their most consequential matters," the firm said in a statement to CNBC. "Following a careful review of strategic alternatives, the Firm's Management Committee has recommended to the partnership that the Firm pursue an orderly wind-down," the firm said. "The partners are expected to vote in the coming days."Weil said that during the wind-down process in coming months, the "firm will continue serving clients with the dedication and excellence that have defined it since its founding and will remain committed to supporting its colleagues."Over the years, Weil had been involved in major bankruptcy filings, including for Lehman Brothers, General Motors and Enron.

schema.headline: Weil, Gotshal & Manges, longtime Wall Street law firm, plans wind down

title: Samsung Electronics shares slid despite record profit in the third-quarter
description: The Samsung logo, representing the South Korean multinational manufacturing conglomerate, the largest chaebol of South Korea, and the world's largest
body: The Samsung logo, representing the South Korean multinational manufacturing conglomerate, the largest chaebol of South Korea, and the world's largest information technology company, consumer electronics maker, chipmaker, and smartphone manufacturer, appears on their pavilion during the Mobile World Congress 2025 in Barcelona, Spain, on March 5, 2025. (Photo by Joan Cros/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesSouth Korean tech giant Samsung Electronics closed 4.13% lower on Thursday, paring earlier losses of as much as 5%, after the company reported third-quarter operating profit broadly in line with analysts' estimates.Here are Samsung's third-quarter results compared with LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate:Revenue: 195.25 trillion won ($124 billion) vs. 195.79 trillion won expected Operating profit: 107.44 trillion won vs. 107.66 trillion won expected  Samsung's revenue rose 126.88% year-on-year and 13.85% from the previous quarter, while operating profit rose 783.11% from a year earlier.The company also announced 30 trillion won in cash dividends for the third quarter, equivalent to 4,601 won per common and preferred share.The company plans to return another 55 trillion to 75 trillion won to shareholders this year through dividends and share buybacks, as the board will finalize the total shareholder returns and specific execution plans at a meeting scheduled for late January 2027.Samsung said it became the first global technology company to top 100 trillion won in quarterly operating profit, while posting record revenue and profit for a fourth straight quarter.Its semiconductor business reported 147.1 trillion won in revenue and 106.5 trillion won in operating profit, driven by strong demand for AI-related memory chips.Furthermore, its memory business also achieved record quarterly revenue and operating profit, supported by a significant ramp-up in HBM4 sales and growing demand for server solid-state drives.However, Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at investment platform eToro, appeared unaroused by the numbers, as the results failing to generate much enthusiasm in the market.The market still was not impressed.Josh GilbertAPAC Lead Analyst, eToro"Investors have been so spoilt by the AI trade that a record result is now treated as the bare minimum rather than a reason to celebrate," Gilbert said, adding that Samsung's chip business accounted for nearly all of its operating profit in the third quarter, highlighting its growing reliance on memory chips."For all the talk of Samsung being a diversified giant, anyone holding the stock today is really holding a memory maker with a phone business attached," he said, stating that the company's fortunes now depend heavily on memory prices.Looking ahead, the company expects AI infrastructure investment to accelerate in 2027, with rising demand likely to further tighten memory supply. Samsung also plans to increase sales of HBM, a type of high-performance memory used in AI chips, along with other memory products used in servers and data storage. In the third quarter, Samsung Electronics and five of its affiliates had announced a combined $1 billion investment in KKR-backed Helix Digital Infrastructure. Samsung Electronics will invest $500 million, with the remaining amount coming from its affiliates.The tech giant had also announced a partnership with French AI startup Mistral AI to use AI technologies in its semiconductor operations, including chip design and manufacturing. The company also led Mistral's Series D funding round.

schema.headline: Samsung Electronics shares slid despite record profit in the third-quarter

title: Merck tops quarterly estimates, hikes profit outlook as new form of Keytruda shows strength
description: The exterior view of the entrance to Merck headquarters in Rahway, New Jersey, on Feb. 5, 2024.Spencer Platt | Getty ImagesMerck on Thursday topped th
body: The exterior view of the entrance to Merck headquarters in Rahway, New Jersey, on Feb. 5, 2024.Spencer Platt | Getty ImagesMerck on Thursday topped third-quarter estimates and hiked its adjusted profit outlook, as its immunotherapy Keytruda, including a newer injectable form of the drug, showed stronger-than-expected sales. The pharmaceutical giant now expects adjusted earnings to be between $2.77 and $2.82 per share. That adjusted profit outlook is up from a previous range of $2.66 to $2.76 per share. The guidance now includes a one-time charge of $400 million, or 12 cents per share, related to its licensing agreement with the Chinese cancer drugmaker SciBrunchMerck also narrowed the low end of its 2026 revenue guidance, now expecting sales between $66.8 billion and $67.3 billion. That compares to a previous outlook of $66.3 billion to $67.3 billion. The company has been on a deal spree as it races to offset generic competition for Keytruda after key patents begin expiring in 2028. Merck is also positioning the new form of the drug, Keytruda Qlex, as a cornerstone of its growth strategy. The goal is to transition patients from the original intravenous version to Qlex, considered a more convenient under-the-skin injection. This strategy allows the company to defend its market share and sustain Keytruda's blockbuster sales beyond the original version's loss of exclusivity.Keytruda raked in $8.60 billion in sales for the quarter, beating the $7.73 billion that analysts were expecting, according to StreetAccount. That includes $830 million in sales for Qlex – the highest seen in a quarter since it launched in 2025. Analysts were expecting $649 million in sales, StreetAccount estimates said. The blowout quarter for the shot suggests it could soon be a blockbuster product, meaning it could rake in more than $1 billion in sales for the company. Here's what Merck reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $2.49 adjusted vs. $2.08 expectedRevenue: $18.09 billion vs. $17.31 billion expectedThe company posted a net income of $5.07 billion, or $2.04 per share, for the quarter. That compares with net income of $5.79 billion, or $2.32 per share, for the year-earlier period. Excluding acquisition and restructuring costs, Merck posted earnings of $2.49 per share for the third quarter.Merck raked in $18.09 billion in revenue for the quarter, up 5% from the same period a year earlier.Beyond Keytruda, Merck's newer products also showed strong growth. Winrevair, which is used to treat a rare, deadly lung condition, generated $694 million in sales for the quarter, up 93% from the same period a year earlier. Analysts were expecting sales of $645 million. Meanwhile, the Gardasil vaccine, which prevents cancers from HPV, a very common sexually transmitted infection, drew about $2 billion in sales due to higher demand in the U.S. That tops the $1.76 billion in sales that analysts were expecting. That strong revenue comes after Merck last year grappled with elevated Gardasil inventory and weak demand for the vaccine in China. Meanwhile, Merck's animal health business posted $1.68 billion in sales for the third quarter, which came in slightly below analysts' estimates.

schema.headline: Merck tops quarterly estimates, hikes profit outlook as new form of Keytruda shows strength

title: Over 41,000 U.S. Homeland Security officials' details apparently exposed after massive data breach
description: The Department of Homeland Security logo is seen on a law enforcement vehicle in Washington, United States on March 7, 2017.Samuel Corum | Anadolu | G
body: The Department of Homeland Security logo is seen on a law enforcement vehicle in Washington, United States on March 7, 2017.Samuel Corum | Anadolu | Getty ImagesThe identities of over 41,000 officials from the Department of Homeland Security have allegedly been exposed in a massive data breach by a hacktivist group calling itself the Department of Peace.Late Wednesday stateside, the database was posted on Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit dedicated to news leaks, with claims that it was obtained from an Okta single sign-on service used by the DHS. It appears to reveal employee names, offices, contact information and assignments, and is searchable. Okta didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.DDoS said that "this is not a comprehensive list of all DHS employees," quoting cofounder Emma Best saying, "Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations."DHS didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The agency told the Washington Post that it was "aware of a potential breach" and was "working to address the situation swiftly and effectively."The searchable database appears to include employees from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Customs and Border Protection and the DHS headquarters. The hacker group said the leak was carried out in response to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin reportedly saying on July 17 that ICE will be "turning up the heat on the streets" by intensifying immigration arrests and traffic stops.In U.S. President Donald Trump's second term, the backlash to his efforts to intensify arrests and deportations of suspected illegal immigrants has increased as ICE agents have been documented using physical force during operations.DHS completed 980,000 deportations in the first 18 months of his term, according to the Migration Policy Institute.

schema.headline: Over 41,000 U.S. Homeland Security officials' details apparently exposed after massive data breach

title: FedEx beats expectations, raises outlook in first report since calendar adjustment
description: A FedEx delivery truck is seen in Chicago, Illinois, July 25, 2026.Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesFedEx on Wednesday reported quarterly earning
body: A FedEx delivery truck is seen in Chicago, Illinois, July 25, 2026.Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesFedEx on Wednesday reported quarterly earnings that beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines and raised its full-year outlook for its newly realigned fiscal year. Shares of the company fell slightly in extended trading.Here's how the company performed for the period ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $3.74 adjusted vs. $3.36 expectedRevenue: $22.86 billion vs. $22.42 billion expectedThe company reported net income for the quarter of $290 million, or $1.21 per share, compared with $650 million, or $2.73 per share, during the comparable period a year prior. Adjusting for one-time items — including losses related to short-term investments, gains on the extinguishment of debt and certain restructuring costs — FedEx reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.74. It marks the first report of FedEx's realigned fiscal year, moving the end of its calendar from May 31 to Dec. 31. The report also comes after the company successfully spun out FedEx Freight into a separate publicly traded company. FedEx said its express U.S. segment operating income increased in the quarter, primarily driven by higher package yields and volume. "As our strong operating results and adjusted free cash flow demonstrate, FedEx is winning across high-value market segments while we optimize our network, driving an increase to our full-year outlook," CEO Raj Subramaniam said in a statement.For the full year, the company is now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $18 and $18.60, compared with a prior range of $16.90 to $18.10. FedEx also said it's revising its 2026 revenue growth expectation to a roughly 12% year-over-year increase, up from previous guidance of an 11% increase.Earlier this week, FedEx named former AutoZone executive Jamere Jackson as the company's new chief financial officer, effective Nov. 30. He replaces Claude Russ, who served as the interim CFO since June 1. John Dietrich was announced as stepping down from that role in April.

schema.headline: FedEx beats expectations, raises outlook in first report since calendar adjustment

title: Hegseth reportedly fires U.S. top military planner as Trump downplays Iran peace talks
description: U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth gives a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30, 2026 in Quantico, Virginia.Alex W
body: U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth gives a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30, 2026 in Quantico, Virginia.Alex Wong | Getty ImagesU.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly fired the Pentagon's top military planner amid concerns that Washington may restart strikes on Iran after the midterm elections. Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Staff, according to the Associated Press. No reason was given for his dismissal, and nobody was named as his replacement. Sylvia has now retired, ABC News reported, citing two people familiar with the matter. The AP also reported that U.S. officials have told some countries in the Middle East to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week's midterm elections, as well as for any Iranian retaliation. Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iran "engaging one of Iran's most powerful hard-liners to revive peace negotiations." Trump downplayed the idea of peace talks, telling reporters, "They need help with medical supplies and various things," adding, "he asked me what I thought. I said, 'If you want to do that, that's OK.'"On Tehran's part, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X late Wednesday that "Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed."He said that Iran remains in "close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week."The 7-day plan was proposed last month, and Tehran said the ​Strait of Hormuz could be reopened and normal maritime passage ​restored if the necessary conditions — which reportedly included ending hostilities and releasing frozen Iranian assets — are met.Tehran then would reopen the Strait to normal commercial shipping and resume negotiations with Washington.

schema.headline: Hegseth reportedly fires U.S. top military planner as Trump downplays Iran peace talks

title: Trump methane policy rollback may have minimal impact on crude prices, EPA says
description: The Valero Houston Refinery in Houston, Texas, US, on Friday, March 13, 2026. The worst supply disruption in the history of the oil market is showing
body: The Valero Houston Refinery in Houston, Texas, US, on Friday, March 13, 2026. The worst supply disruption in the history of the oil market is showing no signs of abating, with crude prices surging since the Iran war began. Photographer: Mark Felix/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesBloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesU.S. President Donald Trump's proposed rollback of methane emissions rules would do little to lower oil and natural gas prices, according to the Environmental Protection Agency’s own economic modeling.Trump and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the proposal Tuesday in Lubbock, Texas, in a bid to lower regulatory costs and support domestic energy production.“When owners and operators can produce, America benefits with lower prices,” Zeldin said in EPA’s announcement. The EPA projects that the changes would lower U.S. crude prices by 11 cents a barrel in 2027, or 0.14%, while increasing domestic oil production by 0.09%. That amounts to roughly one extra barrel for every 1,000 the U.S. would otherwise produce, according to CNBC's calculations.CLSA energy research analyst Baden Moore said uncertainty over implementation and the policy’s durability across administrations could constrain producers’ investment decisions.That “limits the upside to current production rates in the near term,” including in 2027, he told CNBC.He added that the changes could instead slow declines in existing production by allowing some wells to remain operational when environmental compliance costs would otherwise make them uneconomic.Moore anticipates that the policy would affect only a small proportion of the U.S. shale market.With CLSA expecting oil prices to remain above $80 a barrel, many wells would already be commercially viable, limiting the number whose continued operation would depend on regulatory relief.The proposal could help many well operators while having a limited effect on overall supply. Marginal wells — wells that produce small amounts of oil and gas — account for around 80% of active U.S. wells, but less than 10% of production, according to the International Energy Agency.EPA proposal rollbackThe EPA is considering lighter methane requirements based either on a well site’s production levels or whether it uses conventional or unconventional extraction methods.The agency would also scrap its Super Emitter Program, which relies on approved third-party monitors to identify major methane releases. Separately, operators could manage gas produced alongside oil through flaring that destroys 95% of the methane.The EPA projects the proposal would result in an additional 60 million short tons of methane emissions from 2027 through 2050.The agency told CNBC it estimates the changes would save the U.S. economy about $45 billion over that period, including roughly $42 billion in lower compliance costs.The EPA also expects operators to capture less gas for sale or use, resulting in about $4.2 billion in lost revenue. That figure is already reflected in its estimate of $42 billion in compliance savings.This proposal remains subject to the rulemaking process, including a public-comment period and further EPA review, before any changes can be finalized.It comes as the Trump administration has also moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports as part of efforts to address fuel prices. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC Tuesday that additional shipments could be permitted depending on Moscow’s actions.

schema.headline: Trump methane policy rollback may have minimal impact on crude prices, EPA says

title: Analysis: Warsh is learning to wield the Fed's power without showing his hand
description: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh answers questions as he delivers remarks during a news conference following the Federal Open Market Committee meetin
body: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh answers questions as he delivers remarks during a news conference following the Federal Open Market Committee meetings at Federal Reserve Headquarters on October 28, 2026 in Washington, DC. Alex Wong | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesKevin Warsh is done proving himself. The Federal Reserve chairman's press conference Wednesday was sharply different from his early appearances in the job, when he often seemed backed into a corner. He's shown he is willing to let the markets guess where he is going — at least to a point. And he has started using his authority to reshape the institution. Warsh was appointed by a president who said cutting interest rates was a litmus test for his choice for Fed chair. When the Federal Open Market Committee opted to hold rates flat in June and July, even with inflation well above the Fed's 2% target, a swarm of commentators questioned the new chairman's credibility. The FOMC's subsequent decision in September to raise rates came with such a hawkish reading of the economy by Warsh that the markets swung sharply in the opposite direction. Investors thought the Fed might be locked into a rate hike this week until a pair of top officials came out and appeared to deliberately temper market expectations. This week, Warsh put all that behind him. He disavowed any expectation that the Fed is on a set course: "If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today," he said. But Warsh also gave a strong signal that his current lean is toward higher rates. "While overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight," he said.He was preserving his options while laying the intellectual groundwork for a hike in December, should inflation remain stubborn.Warsh declined to confirm the widespread assumption in the markets that the officials who had talked down the markets had done so at his direction. Fed insiders have said that the Fed's vice chairs usually coordinate messaging with the chair. "To suggest somehow that I am some kind of all-knowing person sending messages out, that's not the committee of the FOMC that I know," Warsh said. And yet the market got the message that the Fed wouldn't hike this week. If Warsh wants to give otherwise taboo forward guidance through his lieutenants, he now has plausible deniability. This is Warsh's MO: He is intellectually flexible and highly focused on achieving his goals. For instance, one of the goals of the task forces he has assembled to kick-start policy changes is to change the way the Fed measures inflation. But that was impossible while his commitment to fighting it was in question. September's rate hike does a lot to answer the skeptics who said he wasn't serious about slowing price increases, and he is willing to deliver more rate increases, if necessary. "If you think that we're tolerating some inflation target somewhere in the twos, let us disabuse you of it," Warsh said Wednesday. The target is 2% flat. His remarks are a recipe for higher rates as long as the economy stays strong. Warsh and the FOMC will have a raft of new data before the next meeting, in December, to make their case. That could, alternatively, help him make the case that productivity is rising, allowing for more growth without inflation. Meanwhile, Warsh's other changes at the Fed are starting to take effect. He announced a plan Wednesday to reduce the number of times the FOMC is scheduled to vote on interest rates over the next two years. The Fed will keep meeting eight times a year, but will skip a vote on whether to change rates at one meeting in 2027 and two in 2028. That move has the effect of devaluing a good chunk of Fedspeak. The market won't pay much mind to a marginal regional Fed president's comments when they come as much as three months ahead of a rate decision. Regional presidents also get one fewer scheduled vote in their year-long rotations as decision-makers on the FOMC. The Fed chairman retains the authority to call an impromptu meeting at any time should he see the need to change rates. The Marriner S. Eccles Federal Reserve Board Building is seen under construction in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 15, 2026.Mehmet Eser | Anadolu | Getty ImagesBut there are risks to Warsh's way of doing business, especially as he recedes further behind the curtain. The advocates for Fed transparency believe that sunlight adds more rigor to officials' arguments. That could already be a problem, said Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at asset manager PGIM. He is in the camp that thinks inflation is running too hot to justify the Fed's decision not to raise rates this week."While more data is always better, Warsh did not sufficiently explain why this backdrop did not justify a rate increase, particularly given his comment that while he thinks financial conditions have tightened, he would not say they are tight," Sockin said. It was a "policy mistake" to hold, "and a gradual Fed likely means one that has to hike higher, mechanically raising recession risk," Sockin said.The full consequences of Warsh's approach may not become clear for months. That gives him room to maneuver as he reshapes the Fed. But it also means the consequences of waiting to tighten may not become apparent until it's too late.

schema.headline: Analysis: Warsh is learning to wield the Fed's power without showing his hand

title: Here are five key takeaways from the Fed rate decision and Warsh news conference
description: Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, during a news conference following a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in Washington, DC,
body: Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, during a news conference following a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Al Drago | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to hold its benchmark interest rate steady. At the press conference that followed, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh disclosed some of his thinking about where the U.S. economy stands, and how that affects monetary policy. But for Fed wonks, the big news may have been Warsh's disclosure of some procedural changes ahead.Here are five key takeaways:No surprises: Markets had been widely expecting the Fed to hold, and it did just that. In explaining its decision, the Federal Open Market Committee emphasized a patient approach, saying, "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."Well, one surprise: If there was one eyebrow-raising moment from the afternoon, it was Warsh's disclosure of changes in how the FOMC will meet. In 2027, the committee will still meet eight times, but one of the meetings will not entail a vote on interest rates, or include a post-meeting statement. The "strategy" meetings will increase to two the next year, leaving just six opportunities to adjust rates — outside of emergency meetings.OK, two surprises: The FOMC vote to hold policy where it stands was widely expected. Dissent from multiple members also came as no shock. But one of the "no" votes coming from Governor Lisa Cook was a stunner. Governors rarely dissent from rate votes, and Cook hasn't done so at all since taking her seat in 2022. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack also opposed the decision. Both likely will provide statements explaining their votes before the end of the week.The AI impact: Warsh took the opportunity to talk about the impact artificial intelligence is having on economic growth, essentially saying that it was just one of several factors driving an expansion that he said was running strong.More musical chairs: The September meeting featured a shortened post-meeting news conference — cut from the usual 45 minutes or so down to half an hour, about the time of Wednesday's event. Moreover, reporters have been limited to a single question, a switch from prior practices when media members would take a two-for-one approach. Finally, Warsh has changed the seating in the room, going from a largely arbitrary approach — with representatives of larger outfits up front — to alphabetical order last month. This month featured reverse alphabetical order, keeping the bearers of the microphone on their toes.What they're saying:"The Fed is leaning into patience. It seems they prefer to wait for more information on the appropriate level of rates, as uncertainty reigns supreme in light of recent geopolitical developments." —Phil Camporeale, chief investment strategist, JPMorgan Wealth Management."The Fed has time on its side ... But the direction of travel remains clear. The Fed is still taking back some of last year's rate cuts, and the two dissents underline that tightening bias. We expect a hike in December and another in early 2027." — Seema Shah, chief global strategist, Principal Asset Management."We hesitate to characterize his communication as particularly dovish or hawkish ... The bottom line is that the Fed policy reaction is not a black-and-white, binary thing ... The market has adjusted to Warsh's communication style, but there might be a ways to go before they are fully on the same page." — Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist, Jefferies.
